overall:
System A: 7/11 successes, total 46/55. It ran multi-round agent/tools loops, followed the dependent-call chains, produced every citation string via format_citation (all author lists, years and ids match the catalogue), and reported honestly when Semantic Scholar rate-limited get_citation_count (Q2, Q3, Q9, Q10), which is the only reason it missed those questions. Its weaknesses are efficiency and filtering: 8 unnecessary calls (redundant id/title searches after get_paper, counting off-topic candidates in Q5, citing BERT as a vision paper in Q8). No invented facts.

System B: 1/11 successes (only Q11), total 28/55. In every question it stopped after a single tool round, so it never called get_citation_count or check_citation and called format_citation only when the id was given up front (Q11). It never reported a citation count and never attempted one; in Q10 it falsely claimed it had no citation tool. Its citation strings in Q1, Q6 and Q8 were written from memory (search cards do not carry full author lists), and two of them contradict the catalogue: Q5's ReAct BibTeX invents six co-author names and Q6's GAN BibTeX uses the title 'Generative adversarial nets' plus a venue and pages not in the record. Its one relative strength was relevance judgement (correctly excluding BERT in Q8).
